html:
The Kwakwaka'wakw, "those who speak Kwak'wala", are an Indigenous people of the Pacific Northwest Coast, living on northern Vancouver Island and the facing mainland of British Columbia, Canada. Older books call them the Kwakiutl.

Their villages of cedar plank houses lived off salmon, shellfish and the forest. Society was ranked, with chiefs, nobles and commoners, and wealth and rank were shown at the potlatch, a feast where hosts gave away goods to validate titles and names. They are famous for carved house posts, totem poles and spectacular transformation masks used in winter dances.

Canada banned the potlatch from 1885 to 1951, and in 1921 officials seized regalia after a large potlatch; some has since been returned. The anthropologist Franz Boas, working with George Hunt, a Kwakwaka'wakw man, made them one of the most studied peoples of the world. Neighbours include the Nuu-chah-nulth and the Heiltsuk; the Quatsino are one of their groups.
